person.name: George_Washington
person.summary: George Washington was a Virginia planter who became commander in chief of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. He led American and French forces to victory at Yorktown, chaired the Constitutional Convention, and served as the first president of the United States.

conclusion: Washington’s command at Yorktown secured the military victory that brought American independence. He presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first president under the Constitution. His retirement after two terms established a precedent followed by later presidents for more than a century.

events.title: Birth at Wakefield
events.description: George Washington was born at Wakefield, also called Pope’s Plantation, in Westmoreland County, Virginia. He entered the household of Augustine Washington, a planter and merchant whose wealth came chiefly from land, plantations, and enslaved labor, and Mary Ball Washington, a member of a landholding Virginia family. His older half-siblings Lawrence, Augustine Jr., and Jane were already part of the family from Augustine’s first marriage.

images.caption: Washington family plantation at Popes Creek, Virginia
images.creator: NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Map of Washington’s farm courtesy of the Library of Congress. Story by Adam Voiland.

events.title: Surveys the Shenandoah
events.description: At sixteen, George Washington joined George William Fairfax on a [[land surveying|land-surveying]] expedition through Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. He spent the next three years surveying frontier land, earning income and learning the region’s terrain and property boundaries.

land surveying.explanation: Land surveying measures and maps property boundaries and terrain. In colonial Virginia, the work helped establish land claims and gave Washington practical knowledge of the region.

events.title: Begins Managing Mount Vernon
events.description: After Lawrence Washington died in 1752, George Washington began managing Mount Vernon on the Potomac. He also received an appointment as a militia adjutant in Virginia, beginning his public military service.

images.caption: Mount Vernon Estate, Fairfax County, Virginia
images.creator: ALobato

events.background:
Mount Vernon was the former Little Hunting Creek plantation. Lawrence Washington had renamed it for Admiral Edward Vernon. The estate stood on the Potomac River and comprised 2,126 acres.

Washington’s control of the property developed in stages. Lawrence’s daughter Sarah survived until 1754. Lawrence’s widow Anne retained a life interest in the plantation. She leased Mount Vernon to Washington after her remarriage. Washington inherited the estate outright when Anne died in 1761.

events.title: Carries Dinwiddie's Demand
events.description: George Washington left Williamsburg on Robert Dinwiddie’s mission to demand that French commanders withdraw from forts in the Ohio Valley. The mission failed. Washington published The Journal of Major Washington, an account of the journey and negotiations. Colonial newspapers printed it, and newspapers in England and Scotland reprinted it.

event_class.title: The Journal of Major Washington
event_class.impact: The journal brought Washington public recognition in Virginia, England, and Scotland.

events.title: Surrenders Fort Necessity
events.description: French forces surrounded George Washington’s Virginia militia at [[Fort Necessity|Fort Necessity]] in the Ohio Country, a region claimed by both Britain and France. His men suffered heavy losses while fighting in the rain. Washington signed surrender terms that allowed the surviving troops to withdraw to Virginia.

images.caption: Reconstructed Fort Necessity in southern Pennsylvania
images.creator: Wilson44691

Fort Necessity.explanation: Fort Necessity was a hastily built British stockade in what is now southwestern Pennsylvania. Washington’s force used it as a defensive position during the opening campaign of the French and Indian War.

events.title: Commands Virginia Regiment
events.description: George Washington served as a captain and aide to General Edward Braddock during the British advance toward Fort Duquesne. Braddock was mortally wounded at the Battle of the Monongahela. Washington helped organize the retreat and later became colonel of the Virginia Regiment, commanding Virginia’s frontier defense.
events.background:
Braddock’s army brought a ten-kilometer supply column through 160 kilometers of difficult wilderness. A 950-man force from Fort Duquesne surrounded its vanguard on July 9. About two-thirds of that force were Native American fighters. Virginia troops came under crossfire from British soldiers and Native fighters. Three horses were shot beneath Washington. The expedition lost 900 of its 1,300 men.

Washington drew practical conclusions from the defeat. He believed a large force burdened by artillery and a long supply train could not move effectively against woodland fighters in the Ohio country. His new regiment became Virginia’s first regular unit and sometimes had more than 1,000 men. Its blue uniforms gave it the name the Blues. Washington enforced strict discipline, wrote detailed orders, and trained many recent immigrants from England, Ireland, and Scotland in mobile forest fighting.

Shawnee and Delaware fighters raided English settlements west of the Blue Ridge after the British loss. Washington could not compel them to accept a decisive battle. He sought Catawba and Cherokee allies from the Carolinas, since he considered Native scouts essential in fighting Native forces. Most groups in the region remained aligned with France. Washington therefore maintained a defensive system of forts along the western side of the Blue Ridge.

events.title: Marries Martha Custis
events.description: George Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis at White House Plantation in Virginia. Martha was the widow of planter Daniel Parke Custis. Her inherited estate and business interests became part of the Mount Vernon household.

locations.name_historic: White House Plantation, Colony of Virginia

images.caption: White House Plantation on the Pamunkey River
images.creator: Benson John Lossing

events.title: Commands Continental Army
events.description: On June 15, 1775, the [[Second Continental Congress|Second Continental Congress]], meeting in Philadelphia, appointed George Washington commander in chief of the [[Continental Army|Continental Army]]. Washington accepted command of the American forces besieging the British Army in Boston after John Adams proposed him and Thomas Johnson formally nominated him.

Second Continental Congress.explanation: The colonial legislative body that coordinated the American resistance to Britain and directed the revolutionary war effort. It met in Philadelphia when it appointed Washington commander in chief.

Continental Army.explanation: The army established by the Continental Congress in 1775 to fight British forces during the American Revolutionary War. Washington became its highest-ranking commander.

events.title: Strikes at Trenton
events.description: George Washington led Continental Army soldiers across the ice-filled Delaware River into New Jersey and attacked the [[Hessian troops|German troops serving the British army]] at Trenton. The Americans captured the garrison. The victory restored their position in New Jersey.

Hessian troops.explanation: Hessian troops were soldiers from German states, especially Hesse-Kassel, hired by Britain to fight in the American Revolutionary War. A Hessian garrison occupied Trenton during the attack.

events.title: Endures Valley Forge
events.description: On December 19, 1777, George Washington brought the American revolutionary army into winter quarters at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania. The soldiers faced shortages of food, clothing, shelter, and fuel, while Washington pressed Congress for the supplies and manpower needed to maintain the army.

images.caption: Washington presenting Congress's committee at Valley Forge
images.creator: William Henry Powell

events.title: Wins at Yorktown
events.description: American and French forces under George Washington and [[Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau|the Comte de Rochambeau]] surrounded the British army at Yorktown. French warships under [[François Joseph Paul de Grasse|the Comte de Grasse]] blocked escape through Chesapeake Bay. Charles Cornwallis sent General Charles O’Hara to surrender the army on October 19, 1781.
involved_people: Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte de Rochambeau

images.caption: Surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown, 1781
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided

Jean-Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, comte.explanation: Rochambeau commanded the French expeditionary force that joined Washington’s army in the Yorktown campaign.

François Joseph Paul de Grasse.explanation: De Grasse commanded the French fleet whose victory in Chesapeake Bay prevented British evacuation or reinforcement at Yorktown.

events.background:
Yorktown came after Cornwallis's long campaign through the Southern colonies. His relations with Sir Henry Clinton had been strained by disagreements over the campaign. In Virginia, Lafayette's troops kept pressure on Cornwallis while the allied army moved into position.

The surrender ended significant fighting in North America. Lafayette's article calls Yorktown the Revolutionary War's final major battle and says its outcome secured American independence.

events.title: Resigns His Commission
events.description: George Washington appeared before the Continental Congress in Annapolis, Maryland, and resigned as commander in chief of the Continental Army. He returned military authority to civilian representatives of the states. He then went home to Mount Vernon intending to resume private life.

events.title: Presides at Philadelphia
events.description: Delegates to the [[Constitutional Convention|Constitutional Convention]] elected George Washington of Virginia to preside in Philadelphia. They had gathered to revise the [[Articles of Confederation|Articles of Confederation]], the nation’s existing governing charter. James Madison and Alexander Hamilton supported a new federal government.

images.caption: Washington’s chair from the Constitutional Convention
images.creator: NPS Photo

Constitutional Convention.explanation: The Constitutional Convention was the 1787 federal gathering in Philadelphia that debated the structure of the United States government and produced the proposed Constitution.

Articles of Confederation.explanation: The Articles of Confederation were the United States’ first national governing charter. Their limited federal powers led delegates to seek a new constitutional system in 1787.

events.title: Takes Presidential Oath
events.description: George Washington took the presidential oath on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City. Chancellor Robert Livingston administered the oath before a large crowd. Washington then delivered his first inaugural address in the Senate chamber.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

images.caption: Federal Hall in New York City
images.creator: Ajay Suresh from New York, NY, USA

events.background:
The federal government had been scheduled to begin operating on March 4. Both houses of Congress lacked a quorum that day, so they could not count the electoral votes. The House assembled in sufficient numbers on April 1. The Senate did so on April 6. That day, the two chambers certified Washington’s election. Charles Thomson delivered the official notice to Mount Vernon on April 14.

Washington left two days later with Thomson and David Humphreys. Public receptions followed him through Alexandria, Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Trenton. He entered New York Harbor from Elizabethtown in a small barge manned by 13 pilots. Artillery salutes sounded from nearby vessels and shore batteries. Governor George Clinton met him at Murray’s Wharf, and he was taken to the official residence at 3 Cherry Street.

The ceremony used a Bible from St. John’s Lodge No. 1, whose master, Jacob Morton, acted as marshal. It had been opened to Genesis 49:13. Cheers and a 13-gun salute followed the ceremony. The Constitution left an inaugural address optional. Washington believed he should give one. His 1,419-word speech visibly unsettled him, according to Senator William Maclay, who wrote that he trembled and sometimes struggled to read from the paper.

events.title: Marches Against Rebellion
events.description: George Washington personally led federalized militia forces toward western Pennsylvania to suppress resistance to the whiskey tax. He had called up militias from several states under the [[Militia Act of 1792|1792 federal militia law]] after armed opponents threatened federal officers. The resistance dispersed before the army reached Pittsburgh. Alexander Hamilton and Henry Lee accompanied Washington.

Militia Act of 1792.explanation: The Militia Act of 1792 authorized the president to call state militia units into federal service when laws were opposed by force or could not be enforced through ordinary means. Washington used this authority to assemble the force sent to western Pennsylvania.

events.title: Publishes Farewell Address
events.description: George Washington published his [[Farewell Address]] in Philadelphia near the end of his second presidential term. He revised a 1792 draft prepared by James Madison with help from Alexander Hamilton. The address announced that he would not seek a third term. Newspapers around the country reprinted it almost immediately, followed by pamphlet editions.

event_class.title: George Washington's Farewell Address
event_class.impact: Newspapers across the United States reprinted the address almost immediately, and it subsequently appeared in pamphlet editions.

Farewell Address.explanation: Washington’s 1796 public letter announced that he would retire after his second term. It became a widely circulated statement of his views as he left office.

events.background:
The address grew out of an earlier decision that Washington had postponed. In 1792, James Madison drafted a proposed retirement letter when Washington expected to leave after one term. Disputes between Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson, worsening foreign-policy tensions, and the formation of Federalist and Democratic-Republican camps persuaded him to remain. Four years later, the revised letter also answered public anger over the Jay Treaty, which had alienated part of the country from his administration.

Washington used the letter to argue that the states’ independence, peace, security, prosperity, and liberty depended on their union. He asked readers to place an American identity above state and regional attachments. He warned that domestic and foreign adversaries would try to weaken the constitutional union. He also argued that union could spare the country wars among neighboring nations and reduce pressure for a large standing military.

His advice extended to the new constitutional system. He urged obedience to the Constitution unless it was changed by constitutional means. He warned that political parties could open a path to despotism, corruption, and foreign influence. He treated morality, religion, and education as supports for popular government. In foreign affairs, he urged good faith and justice toward every nation. He advised temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies and cautioned against permanent alliances.

events.title: Dies at Mount Vernon
events.description: After riding near Mount Vernon through cold, wet weather on December 12, George Washington developed a severe sore throat. His condition worsened despite treatment by physicians James Craik, Gustavus Richard Brown, and Elisha C. Dick. He died at Mount Vernon on December 14, with Martha Washington and Tobias Lear nearby.
